This is based on a false conclusion.

A teaspoon (made of homogeneous metal) dunked in hot liquid will get hot. Leave it in there, then touch the hot end and it will be... hot. Leave it in there for a long time, and it will build heat up through the rest of it.

What's happening is the bottom of the spoon is absorbing heat, the top is venting that heat to the air (or your fingers). It's not going to be one single temperature throughout the spoon.

Drop the spoon completely submerged into a pot of hot water, and the whole spoon will then be hot.
First non sarcastic answer that made sense, thank you stranger!

Also, saying metals conduct heat is over-generalized. Assuming you are using a normal stainless steel spoon, you need to pay attention to the fact that stainless conducts heat VERY poorly for a metal. That's why good stainless pans have aluminum or copper inserts in the bottom. The stainless radiates heat through the handle quicker than it can move through the spoon.

If you find literal silverware (made of silver) and take the spoon from it and put it in the same drink as your other spoon, you will notice that the silver one's handle gets quite hot, hotter than the one you had.

"Thermal gradient" is the idea you're looking for.

Some materials, like wood or plastic, have a very high thermal gradient- you can stick a spoon of either in a fire, and the other end won't heat up at all, but a spoon of gold or copper- which have very low thermal gradients- will heat up quickly.

Your spoon is probably steel, which has a fairly low thermal gradient for metal.

I think it's for the same reason aluminum foil "never gets hot". You line your cookie sheet with foil and cook something with it at 400 degrees, take it out, and 5 seconds later it's cool to the touch. Ah ok, so I believe what you're asking is when you place a teaspoon in tea, why doesn't the handle-end not get hot?

So, we'll establish that the spoon-end does get hot, and since the handle is made of metal, it should conduct heat and become hot as well.

Basically, it doesn't get hot because it loses the heat through convection to the air. So essentially, you've got hot in at spoon end, and hot out at the spoon-end just above the tea. It's basically all about the air. Heat leaves tea better through air than a small metal spoon stuck in the tea.

BUT, if you did want the handle of the spoon to get as hot as the tea, then you'd have to place the system consisting of the tea and the spoon inside a vacuumed out adiabatic chamber and allow the system to equilibrate. Note: a vacuum chamber is needed because there's no air, so no convective heat transfer occurs. Also, for those that don't know, adiabatic basically means that no heat enters or leaves the system.

This is truly a thermodynamics question being asked, and kind of cool too!
